techniques.name: Algorithm Review Boards
techniques.description: An algorithm review board, also called an AI ethics board or AI review board, is a standing group from different disciplines that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects before they proceed. It differs from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because it also weighs harms to the people a system will affect and to society. Many boards first sort projects by risk, and for higher-risk work the project team submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, which members with technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds question and iterate on with the team. Where it has the power to decide, the board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects; where it only advises, it recommends one of these. It keeps a dated record of its decision, reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built, and some organisations share that record with an oversight body or publish it.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group's algorithm review board examines a sepsis early-warning model before a ward pilot. It approves the pilot on condition of a monitoring plan for alert rates and missed cases, names who may switch the model off, and sets a re-review once six months of local performance data are in, before any wider roll-out.

A bank's board reviews a proposed credit-limit model before launch. It asks the team for its disparate-impact analysis by protected group and for evidence that applicants can contest a decision, and withholds approval until both are supplied, so the decision to deploy rests with a body outside the development team.

A university AI research programme releases grant funding only after each project has passed an ethics and society review, in which researchers state the risks their work poses to society and to particular groups, commit to mitigations, and revise them with an interdisciplinary faculty panel.

A government department publishes the board's decision record for a benefits-triage tool, giving the reasons for approval, the conditions attached and the re-review date, so that its oversight committee and the public can see what was examined, by whom and when, and check later that the conditions were met.

limitations.description: Review adds time and cost to every project that goes through it, and organisations under commercial pressure may route work around the board or narrow its remit, so the board's coverage, not just its existence, needs to be shown.

Its judgements are only as good as its membership. A board without the relevant technical, domain or community expertise will miss harms that fall outside what its members know, and a board drawn mainly from inside the team's own reporting line is open to group-think.

Independence is hard to keep inside an organisation. Practitioners report tension between profit and the cost of responsible-AI review, and a board can come under pressure to approve projects that leadership has already committed to, which weakens it most where review matters most.

Without authority to stop or delay a project, and a way to check that its conditions are met, a board's recommendations can be ignored. Evidence from a board is strong only when its decision record shows what it could block and what happened to its conditions.

There is no agreed measure of whether a board works, and review can become box-ticking. A record that a project was reviewed shows that a process ran, not that the review was substantive or that its concerns were addressed.

resources.title: Looking before we leap: Expanding ethical review processes for AI and data science research
resources.abstract: Expanding ethical review processes for AI and data science research

resources.title: How to design an AI ethics board
resources.abstract: The development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems poses significant risks to society. To reduce these risks to an acceptable level, AI companies need an effective risk management process and sound risk governance. In this paper, we explore a particular way in which AI companies can improve their risk governance: by setting up an AI ethics board. We identify five key design choices: (1) What responsibilities should the board have? (2) What should its legal structure be? (3) Who should sit on the board? (4) How should it make decisions? (5) And what resources does it need? We break each of these questions down into more specific sub-questions, list options, and discuss how different design choices affect the board’s ability to reduce societal risks from AI. Several failures have shown that designing an AI ethics board can be challenging. This paper provides a toolbox that can help AI companies to overcome these challenges.

resources.title: Designing Artificial Intelligence Review Boards: Creating Risk Metrics for Review of AI
resources.abstract: Discussions of the need for a review committee dedicated to ethical oversight of artificial intelligence (AI) research have not yet advanced to organization design discussions. What are the essential components for an AI research review board? Based upon precedent for composition and conduct of high-technology review boards, one essential component is a risk-adjusted review mechanism that assists review boards in the categorization of research needing review. In this paper, risk assessment tools are developed based upon lessons learned from other review boards, such as Institutional Biosafety Committees.

resources.title: Ethics and society review: Ethics reflection as a precondition to research funding
resources.abstract: Researchers in areas as diverse as computer science and political science must increasingly navigate the possible risks of their research to society. However, the history of medical experiments on vulnerable individuals influenced many research ethics reviews to focus exclusively on risks to human subjects rather than risks to human society. We describe an Ethics and Society Review board (ESR), which fills this moral gap by facilitating ethical and societal reflection as a requirement to access grant funding: Researchers cannot receive grant funding from participating programs until the researchers complete the ESR process for their proposal. Researchers author an initial statement describing their proposed research’s risks to society, subgroups within society, and globally and commit to mitigation strategies for these risks. An interdisciplinary faculty panel iterates with the researchers to refine these risks and mitigation strategies. We describe a mixed-method evaluation of the ESR over 1 y, in partnership with an artificial intelligence grant program run by Stanford HAI. Surveys and interviews of researchers who interacted with the ESR found 100% (95% CI: 87 to 100%) were willing to continue submitting future projects to the ESR, and 58% (95% CI: 37 to 77%) felt that it had influenced the design of their research project. The ESR panel most commonly identified issues of harms to minority groups, inclusion of diverse stakeholders in the research plan, dual use, and representation in datasets. These principles, paired with possible mitigation strategies, offer scaffolding for future research designs.

resources.title: ESR Process & Toolkit — Stanford Ethics & Society Review
resources.abstract: The Ethics and Society Review is improving ethical reflection in research by bringing together a panel of ethics experts to help researchers identify and mitigate negative ethical or societal aspects of their research and elevate the positive.

resources.title: Investigating Algorithm Review Boards for Organizational Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance
resources.abstract: Organizations are increasingly developing and utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Responsible AI (RAI) governance approaches including algorithm review board (ARBs) have emerged as important mechanisms to address potential AI risks and harms. We interviewed 17 technical contributors at a variety of organizations about their experiences with internal RAI governance. We summarized the first detailed findings on ARBs in practice, including their membership, scope, and measures of success. We confirmed known ARBs in finance sectors and revealed extensive use of ARBs in health sectors. Our findings suggest that Institutional Review Boards alone are insufficient for algorithm governance and that ARBs are used in tandem with other RAI approaches. Integration with existing processes and leadership buy-in were considered critical to the success of internal RAI governance. Financial tensions between profit and the cost of RAI were a major concern for many participants. Future work should explore measurements of success for ARBs and expand analysis of ARBs to other industries leading in AI implementation.

resources.title: A framework for the oversight and local deployment of safe and high-quality prediction models
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence/machine learning models are being rapidly developed and used in clinical practice. However, many models are deployed without a clear understanding of clinical or operational impact and frequently lack monitoring plans that can detect potential safety signals. There is a lack of consensus in establishing governance to deploy, pilot, and monitor algorithms within operational healthcare delivery workflows. Here, we describe a governance framework that combines current regulatory best practices and lifecycle management of predictive models being used for clinical care. Since January 2021, we have successfully added models to our governance portfolio and are currently managing 52 models.

sample_claims.text: Every high-risk AI system was reviewed and approved by the organisation's algorithm review board before operational use, and the board could have blocked deployment
The conditions the review board attached to the credit-limit model's approval, including a disparate-impact analysis by protected group and a re-review date, were met before and after launch
The clinical decision-support model was deployed under a monitoring plan and re-review schedule set by a multidisciplinary review board independent of the development team
The diagnostic AI system's development and deployment decisions are traceable to dated board decision records that state the risks assessed, the reasons for approval and the conditions attached
The review board's decision record for the risk assessment tool, with its reasons and conditions, is available to the oversight body and the public

techniques.name: Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
techniques.description: Path-specific counterfactual fairness assessment tests whether a protected attribute, such as sex or race, influences a decision along routes that the assessor judges unfair. The assessor first draws a causal graph, a diagram of which variables influence which, and marks each route from the protected attribute to the decision as acceptable or unacceptable. In a classic admissions example, women applied more often to departments with low admission rates, so the effect of sex through department choice was treated as acceptable, while any direct effect of sex was not. The technique then estimates how the decision would change if the protected attribute were switched, counting only the effect that travels along the unacceptable routes. A large estimate points to unfair influence along those routes, and the estimate is only as sound as the graph and the choice of routes.

example_use_cases.description: A company auditing its CV-screening model draws a causal graph from gender to the shortlisting decision. Routes through qualifications are marked acceptable, while the direct route and the route through career-break length are marked unacceptable. The estimated effect along the unacceptable routes tells the audit team whether the model disadvantages women beyond what job-relevant qualifications explain.

A research team auditing ventilation decisions in intensive care uses recorded patient data to estimate how much of the effect of patient race on starting invasive ventilation passes through pulse-oximeter readings, which tend to overstate oxygen levels in dark-skinned patients, and how much through other routes.

limitations.description: Which routes count as unacceptable is a value judgement the assessor must make and defend, and different reasonable choices give different verdicts on the same model. The technique does not settle that question. It only measures the effect along the routes it is given.

The causal graph comes from domain knowledge and cannot be fully checked against observational data. If the graph has a wrong arrow or omits a relevant variable, the assessment can certify an unfair model as compliant, and nothing inside the method flags the error.

Path-specific effects are often not identifiable from observational data alone. When unobserved confounders sit between the protected attribute and the mediating variables or the outcome, the effect along a specific route cannot be uniquely recovered without further parametric assumptions, so the result becomes a bound rather than a point estimate.

Estimating the effect along a route means fitting a model for each variable on it. Outside linear or low-dimensional settings the calculation is hard and relies on approximations, and the answer is only as good as the fitted model's match to the data.
An average effect can hide opposing individual effects. A population-level result does not establish the paper's individual counterfactual criterion for every person.

resources.title: Causal Fairness Analysis — faircause vignettes
faircause: Causal Fairness Analysis (dplecko/CFA)
Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of learning fair decision systems from data in which a sensitive attribute might affect the decision along both fair and unfair pathways. We introduce a counterfactual approach to disregard effects along unfair pathways that does not incur in the same loss of individual-specific information as previous approaches. Our method corrects observations adversely affected by the sensitive attribute, and uses these to form a decision. We leverage recent developments in deep learning and approximate inference to develop a VAE-type method that is widely applicable to complex nonlinear models.

resources.title: A Causal Framework for Discovering and Removing Direct and Indirect Discrimination
resources.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the problem of discovering both direct and indirect discrimination from the historical data, and removing the discriminatory effects before the data is used for predictive analysis (e.g., building classifiers). The main drawback of existing methods is that they cannot distinguish the part of influence that is really caused by discrimination from all correlated influences. In our approach, we make use of the causal network to capture the causal structure of the data. Then we model direct and indirect discrimination as the path-specific effects, which accurately identify the two types of discrimination as the causal effects transmitted along different paths in the network. Based on that, we propose an effective algorithm for discovering direct and indirect discrimination, as well as an algorithm for precisely removing both types of discrimination while retaining good data utility. Experiments using the real dataset show the effectiveness of our approaches.

resources.title: Causal Fairness Analysis: A Causal Toolkit for Fair Machine Learning
resources.abstract: Decision-making systems based on AI and machine learning have been used throughout a wide range of real-world scenarios, including healthcare, law enforcement, education, and finance. It is no longer far-fetched to envision a future where autonomous systems will drive entire business decisions and, more broadly, support large-scale decision-making infrastructure to solve society’s most challenging problems. Issues of unfairness and discrimination are pervasive when decisions are being made by humans, and remain (or are potentially amplified) when decisions are made using machines with little transparency, accountability, and fairness. In this monograph, we introduce a framework for causal fairness analysis with the intent of filling in this gap, i.e., understanding, modeling, and possibly solving issues of fairness in decision-making settings. The main insight of our approach will be to link the quantification of the disparities present in the observed data with the underlying, often unobserved, collection of causal mechanisms that generate the disparity in the first place, a challenge we call the Fundamental Problem of Causal Fairness Analysis (FPCFA). In order to solve the FPCFA, we study the problem of decomposing variations and empirical measures of fairness that attribute such variations to structural mechanisms and different units of the population. Our effort culminates in the Fairness Map, the first systematic attempt to organize and explain the relationship between various criteria found in the literature. Finally, we study which causal assumptions are minimally needed for performing causal fairness analysis and propose the Fairness Cookbook, which allows one to assess the existence of disparate impact and disparate treatment.

resources.title: Causal Fairness Analysis vignette: Census bias detection
Path-specific effects for pulse-oximetry guided decisions in critical care
resources.abstract: Identifying and measuring biases associated with sensitive attributes is a crucial consideration in healthcare to prevent treatment disparities. One prominent issue is inaccurate pulse oximeter readings, which tend to overestimate oxygen saturation for dark-skinned patients and misrepresent supplemental oxygen needs. Most existing research has revealed statistical disparities linking device measurement errors to patient outcomes in intensive care units (ICUs) without causal formalization. This study causally investigates how racial discrepancies in oximetry measurements affect invasive ventilation in ICU settings. We employ a causal inference-based approach using path-specific effects to isolate the impact of bias by race on clinical decision-making. To estimate these effects, we leverage a doubly robust estimator, propose its self-normalized variant for improved sample efficiency, and provide novel finite-sample guarantees. Our methodology is validated on semi-synthetic data and applied to two large real-world health datasets: MIMIC-IV and eICU. Contrary to prior work, our analysis reveals minimal impact of racial discrepancies on invasive ventilation rates. However, path-specific effects mediated by oxygen saturation disparity are more pronounced on ventilation duration, and the severity differs across datasets. Our work provides a novel pipeline for investigating potential disparities in clinical decision-making and, more importantly, highlights the necessity of causal methods to robustly assess fairness in healthcare.

sample_claims.text: The effect of applicant gender on shortlisting along the routes judged unacceptable, the direct route and the route through career-break length, is statistically indistinguishable from zero.
Switching an applicant's ethnicity changes the modelled approval probability by less than the agreed tolerance along every route the review panel marked as unacceptable.

The share of the effect of patient race on the decision to start invasive ventilation that passes through pulse-oximeter readings is estimated, with a stated confidence interval, from the hospital records.

techniques.name: Constitutional AI Evaluation
techniques.description: Constitutional AI evaluation checks whether a language model follows the written principles, or 'constitution', that it was trained or instructed to follow. The evaluator writes test prompts for each principle, and can add prompts where two principles conflict or where a user tries to talk the model out of a principle. A judge, either human reviewers or a second language model whose accuracy has been checked, assesses each response against one principle at a time, often by comparing it with a baseline model's response. The result is a rate for each principle, such as how often the model's response is preferred to the baseline's, which shows which principles it follows well on the prompts tested and which it does not. A fuller evaluation also checks that following the principles has not made the model over-cautious or less capable.

example_use_cases.description: A developer tuning a general-purpose assistant on a constitution that includes 'refuse requests for illegal activity' writes test prompts for each principle, including borderline chemistry-education questions and attempts to extract synthesis instructions. Reviewers compare the tuned model's answers with the base model's, to decide whether the constitution is ready to ship or needs principles rewritten.

A news publisher using an AI summariser governed by a neutrality principle gives it the same contested story framed from several political positions. Reviewers from differing viewpoints score whether each summary adds editorial language, and the editors use the rate by topic to decide where the summariser can run without a human check.

A digital health provider tests a mental health support chatbot built on the principle 'be supportive, but never diagnose' with scripted crisis conversations in which users ask directly for a diagnosis. Clinicians score each reply, and the share that stays on the right side of the boundary decides whether the chatbot is cleared for a limited pilot.

An education company checks a homework assistant built on the principle 'guide learning without giving direct answers' across subjects, age bands and frustrated or urgent requests. It counts replies that simply give the answer, and uses the rate for each subject to decide where the principle needs strengthening before a school rollout.

limitations.description: Principles are written in natural language, so compliance depends on how the judge reads them. Vague principles, or ones that mean different things across cultures and languages, give scores that reviewers would dispute, so the judge's reading needs checking against human reviewers for each principle.

Principles can conflict in complex scenarios, and the evaluation has to decide which should win. If the intended priority is not written down, a model can look compliant on each principle separately and still resolve conflicts differently from what the developer intended.

Adherence is uneven across kinds of principle. In one study of small fine-tuned models, negatively framed principles such as avoiding harmful content were followed much better than positively framed, abstract ones such as benefiting humanity, so an average score can hide principles the model largely ignores.

Scores depend on the test prompts and on the judge. Prompts that miss a principle's edge cases give a falsely high rate, and an automated judge can favour one response position or misapply the principle, so it needs checking against human judgement in each new domain.

When principles are revised after deployment, results must be re-run, and comparing them across principle versions is hard because a change in score may come from the model, the principles or the test criteria.

resources.abstract: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company that's working to build reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems.

resources.abstract: Robust recipes to align language models with human and AI preferences

resources.title: C3AI: Crafting and Evaluating Constitutions for Constitutional AI
resources.abstract: Constitutional AI (CAI) guides LLM behavior using constitutions, but identifying which principles are most effective for model alignment remains an open challenge. We introduce the C3AI framework (Crafting Constitutions for CAI models), which serves two key functions: (1) selecting and structuring principles to form effective constitutions before fine-tuning; and (2) evaluating whether fine-tuned CAI models follow these principles in practice. By analyzing principles from AI and psychology, we found that positively framed, behavior-based principles align more closely with human preferences than negatively framed or trait-based principles. In a safety alignment use case, we applied a graph-based principle selection method to refine an existing CAI constitution, improving safety measures while maintaining strong general reasoning capabilities. Interestingly, fine-tuned CAI models performed well on negatively framed principles but struggled with positively framed ones, in contrast to our human alignment results. This highlights a potential gap between principle design and model adherence. Overall, C3AI provides a structured and scalable approach to both crafting and evaluating CAI constitutions.

resources.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
resources.abstract: As AI systems become more capable, we would like to enlist their help to supervise other AIs. We experiment with methods for training a harmless AI assistant through self-improvement, without any human labels identifying harmful outputs. The only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles, and so we refer to the method as 'Constitutional AI'. The process involves both a supervised learning and a reinforcement learning phase. In the supervised phase we sample from an initial model, then generate self-critiques and revisions, and then finetune the original model on revised responses. In the RL phase, we sample from the finetuned model, use a model to evaluate which of the two samples is better, and then train a preference model from this dataset of AI preferences. We then train with RL using the preference model as the reward signal, i.e. we use 'RL from AI Feedback' (RLAIF). As a result we are able to train a harmless but non-evasive AI assistant that engages with harmful queries by explaining its objections to them. Both the SL and RL methods can leverage chain-of-thought style reasoning to improve the human-judged performance and transparency of AI decision making. These methods make it possible to control AI behavior more precisely and with far fewer human labels.

resources.title: Constitutional AI with Open LLMs
resources.abstract: We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.

resources.title: Domain-Specific Constitutional AI: Enhancing Safety in LLM-Powered Mental Health Chatbots
resources.abstract: Mental health applications have emerged as a critical area in computational health, driven by rising global rates of mental illness, the integration of AI in psychological care, and the need for scalable solutions in underserved communities. These include therapy chatbots, crisis detection, and wellness platforms handling sensitive data, requiring specialized AI safety beyond general safeguards due to emotional vulnerability, risks like misdiagnosis or symptom exacerbation, and precise management of vulnerable states to avoid severe outcomes such as self-harm or loss of trust. Despite AI safety advances, general safeguards inadequately address mental health-specific challenges, including crisis intervention accuracy to avert escalations, therapeutic guideline adherence to prevent misinformation, scale limitations in resource-constrained settings, and adaptation to nuanced dialogues where generics may introduce biases or miss distress signals. We introduce an approach to apply Constitutional AI training with domain-specific mental health principles for safe, domain-adapted CAI systems in computational mental health applications.

resources.title: Collective Constitutional AI: Aligning a Language Model with Public Input
resources.abstract: There is growing consensus that language model (LM) developers should not be the sole deciders of LM behavior, creating a need for methods that enable the broader public to collectively shape the behavior of LM systems that affect them. To address this need, we present Collective Constitutional AI (CCAI): a multi-stage process for sourcing and integrating public input into LMs—from identifying a target population to sourcing principles to training and evaluating a model. We demonstrate the real-world practicality of this approach by creating what is, to our knowledge, the first LM fine-tuned with collectively sourced public input and evaluating this model against a baseline model trained with established principles from a LM developer. Our quantitative evaluations demonstrate several benefits of our approach: the CCAI-trained model shows lower bias across nine social dimensions compared to the baseline model, while maintaining equivalent performance on language, math, and helpful-harmless evaluations. Qualitative comparisons of the models suggest that the models differ on the basis of their respective constitutions, e.g., when prompted with contentious topics, the CCAI-trained model tends to generate responses that reframe the matter positively instead of a refusal. These results demonstrate a promising, tractable pathway toward publicly informed development of language models.

sample_claims.text: On the evaluation's test prompts, the assistant refuses requests for harmful information while still answering legitimate educational queries
Across the scripted crisis conversations, the support chatbot keeps to its boundary between supportive information and medical diagnosis
Across the matched test stories, the news summariser adds editorial language no more often for one political position than for another
The homework assistant keeps to its principle of guiding learning without giving direct answers when users express frustration or urgency, at the rate set in the release criteria

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

resources.title: Closing the AI accountability gap
FAT* Worked Examples: SMACTR internal audit templates (Smile Detection)

sample_claims.text: The claims-triage model was audited before launch by a team outside its product line, through all five SMACTR stages, and the audit report and design history file are held where the risk committee can inspect them.
Every risk rated high in the audit's ethical risk analysis chart has a remediation action agreed with the engineering team and recorded as completed, or formally accepted, before release.
The tests run in the audit's Testing stage were selected from the failure modes ranked highest in the FMEA, and each result is traced to the failure mode it tests.
The documentation the audit required, including a datasheet for the chatbot's fine-tuning data and a model card, was complete before testing began, as recorded in the audit checklist.
